items.title: Reading a two-way quote
items.core_explanation_md:
A dealer rarely gives one price. A quote such as USD/INR 83.2450/83.2550 carries two: the rate at which the **quoting bank buys** a dollar (the bid, 83.2450) and the rate at which it **sells** one (the offer, 83.2550). Both sides are named from the bank's point of view, never the customer's.

India uses the direct method: one unit of foreign currency is priced in a varying number of rupees. Under a direct quote the bank buys low and sells high. So an exporter's dollars are bought on the bid side and an importer's dollars are sold on the offer side; for customers the bank then moves each side further in its own favour by an exchange margin. The rates here are illustrative.
items.expanded_explanation_md:
An indirect quote turns the picture round: the home currency is the fixed unit (for example ₹100) and the number of foreign currency units varies. In the international market the pound, the euro, the Australian dollar and the New Zealand dollar are quoted this way against the US dollar: one unit of that currency for so many dollars.

The dealer's rule turns round as well. With an indirect quote the bank quotes the lower figure when it sells, because handing over fewer foreign units for the same amount of home currency is the dearer price.

items.title: Who is in the forex market, and what each is there for
items.core_explanation_md:
The foreign exchange market has no building. It is a web of dealing rooms and screens that passes business from centre to centre round the clock, Monday to Friday: Tokyo and Sydney first, then Singapore, India and the Gulf, then Frankfurt and London, and New York last. Most deals are struck over the counter, by phone or on electronic platforms.

Three kinds of player meet there:

- **The steerer.** A central bank manages the country's reserves and steps in to calm swings in its own currency.
- **The price makers and go-betweens.** Large commercial banks quote a buying and a selling rate at the same time, deal for customers and for their own books, and take views on rates. Brokers act as middlemen between the others.
- **The users.** Investment funds, companies and individuals come for a reason outside the market: investing abroad, hedging, paying for trade, travel.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why does it matter who is on the other side? Because the motive tells you how to read the move. A bank that quotes both sides all day gives the market its depth: a caller can deal either way at once. A central bank dealing in size is usually not chasing a profit; it is smoothing the value of the home currency.

items.title: Forward rate from spot rate and forward margin
items.core_explanation_md:
A forward rate is built, not guessed: take today's spot rate and adjust it by the forward margin for the period. If the foreign currency costs more for future delivery than for spot, it is at a **premium** and the margin is added. If it costs less, it is at a **discount** and the margin is subtracted.

The two currencies of a pair always mirror each other: when the dollar is at a premium against the rupee, the rupee is at a discount against the dollar.
items.expanded_explanation_md: What sets the margin? Mainly the gap between interest rates in the two currencies, together with expected demand and supply for them. So a forward rate is an expectation written into today's prices. It is not a promise about where the spot rate will stand on that date.

items.title: Value dates: when the money actually moves
items.core_explanation_md:
Agreeing a rate and exchanging the money are two different moments. The day the currencies really change hands is the **value date**, and its name tells you how far it is from the deal date:

| Name | Money moves |
| --- | --- |
| Cash (ready) | the same day |
| Tom | the next working day |
| Spot | the second working day |
| Forward | any day after spot |

Spot is the market's normal basis, and other rates for a currency are built from the spot rate. Count **working** days: a Saturday, Sunday or holiday in a centre where the currency is settled pushes the date to the next working day.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why two days for spot? Deals are struck across time zones, and both banks need time to instruct payment in two different countries. A deal done for an earlier date than spot (cash or tom) or a later one (forward) is priced by adjusting the spot rate.

self_check.prompt_text: Without looking: name the four value dates in order and say what happens when the date falls on a weekend.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cash (same day), tom (next working day), spot (second working day), forward (any later day). A weekend or holiday moves settlement to the next working day.

items.title: What moves an exchange rate: slow forces, frictions and expectations
items.core_explanation_md:
Three kinds of pressure act on a currency, and they work on different clocks.

- **Fundamentals** are the slow forces that come from the economy and its policies: the balance of payments (a surplus tends to strengthen the home currency, a deficit to weaken it), growth, fiscal and monetary policy, interest rates and political stability. They shape the rate over the long run.
- **Technical reasons** are frictions in how money is allowed to move: government controls that hold a currency at an unrealistic value, and freedom or restriction on capital flows. Capital tends to move from lower-yielding to higher-yielding currencies.
- **Speculation** is expectation turned into deals: if a fall is expected, players buy the foreign currency now, and the belief can spread and move the rate by itself.
items.expanded_explanation_md:
Interest rates cut both ways. A rise in domestic rates tends to pull in overseas capital, so the currency firms up in the short term. Kept high for long, the same rates slow the economy, and that weakens the currency over time.

Speculation is not only a threat: speculative deals also add depth and liquidity to the market.

items.title: Who deals, who watches, who settles
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank's foreign exchange dealing room does more than trade. It serves customers and other branches, manages the bank's foreign currency assets and liabilities and its Nostro accounts, and can also take positions for profit.

The one rule that holds the arrangement together is **separation of duties**. Three functions are kept apart:

- **Front office**: the dealers who quote and deal.
- **Mid office**: measures and watches the risk the dealers take, supplies market information, and helps ensure compliance. It stands independent of the dealers.
- **Back office**: confirms and settles deals, does the accounting and reconciles accounts. It both supports the dealers and checks them.

No single person should be able to deal, record and settle the same transaction. That is what stops a mistake, or a worse act, from going unseen.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Ask of any task: is it taking the risk, measuring the risk, or recording what happened? Dealing is the first, risk monitoring and limit checks the second, and confirmation, settlement and reconciliation the third. A lax back office can cancel the dealers' profits or let wrongdoing pass unnoticed, which is why it is given a checking role and not only a clerical one.

items.title: Five ways a dealing room can lose money
items.core_explanation_md:
Managing a dealing room means knowing what can go wrong. Five risks matter:

- **Operational**: people, systems or procedures fail: an error, a breakdown, a missing control.
- **Exchange**: rates move, or receivables and payables in a currency do not match.
- **Credit**: the other side cannot or will not perform. Two stages: *before maturity* (you must replace the deal at today's market rates with a new counterparty) and *during settlement* (one side has paid and the other has not).
- **Liquidity**: liabilities fall due faster than assets can be turned into cash, because maturities do not match.
- **Market**: rates or prices move against you and you cannot get out in time. It shows up as interest rate, equity price and currency risk.

The board of a bank is expected to set a policy and limits for dealing; the five risks are what those limits are meant to contain.

self_check.prompt_text: A counterparty fails while a deal is still open and before any money has moved. Which of the five risks has arisen, and what does the bank now have to do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Credit risk, at the pre-settlement stage: the bank must cover the transaction at current market rates with a new counterparty.

items.title: Forward or future: who writes the terms, and who stands behind the deal
items.core_explanation_md:
A derivative is a product whose value is derived from something else, such as a currency position. Used to take a view it is speculation; used to cut the risk in everyday cash flows it is hedging.

Two derivatives fix a future exchange rate today, and they differ on two questions.

- **Who writes the terms?** A **forward** is negotiated between a customer and a bank, in any size and for the dates they agree. A **future** is a standard contract, in a fixed size, traded on an exchange.
- **Who stands behind it?** In a forward you rely on the other party, and no collateral is demanded explicitly. In a future the clearing house sits between buyer and seller and guarantees both, and it protects itself by collecting margins.

A forward is typically settled by delivery or cancellation on the due date. A future is usually closed out by taking an opposite position.
items.expanded_explanation_md: That is why a forward is the usual tool for an exporter or importer with a known amount and date: it can be tailored. The standard future suits those who want a traded, guaranteed contract and can manage margin calls.

items.title: Options: a right you pay for
items.core_explanation_md:
An option gives its buyer the **right, not the obligation**, to buy or sell currency at a fixed price during a set period. Because the buyer can walk away, the buyer pays for the right: the **premium**.

- A **call** is a right to buy; a **put** is a right to sell. In currency business calls tend to suit importers and puts exporters.
- The buyer is the **holder**; the seller is the **writer** (or grantor).
- The fixed price is the **strike** (exercise) price.
- An **American** option can be exercised at any time up to expiry; a **European** option only on the expiry date.

Compare the strike with today's spot rate, ignoring the premium: if exercising now would pay, the option is **in the money**; if not, **out of the money**; if strike and spot are equal, **at the money**.

self_check.prompt_text: An importer holds a call on dollars with a strike of 84.00. Spot is 84.50. Is the option in, at or out of the money, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In the money: exercising lets the importer buy at 84.00 what costs 84.50 in the market, a gain before the premium.

items.title: Four swaps told apart by what changes hands
items.core_explanation_md:
A swap is an agreement to exchange streams of cash flows. The useful question for each variety is: *what is on each leg?*

- **Currency swap**: one leg is in one currency, the other in another. It can hedge exchange rate risk and interest rate risk in a single arrangement.
- **Zero coupon swap**: the fixed leg pays nothing along the way and settles in one payment at the end, while the other party keeps paying its floating rate regularly.
- **Equity swap**: one leg follows the return on a reference equity, the other a fixed-income flow such as a benchmark interest rate. Each party gets the exposure it wants without selling the assets it holds.
- **Basis swap**: both legs are floating, but tied to *different* floating rates.

Compare with the plain interest rate swap you have already met, where one leg is fixed and the other floating.

items.title: A dealer's two books: funds and currency
items.core_explanation_md:
A dealer watches two positions at once, and each hides a different risk.

- **Funds position**: money coming in and going out, receivables and payables. If they do not match, the bank either funds a gap by overdrawing a Nostro account and pays interest, or sits on surplus credit balances and loses interest. The risk is an **interest** cost.
- **Currency position**: the net holding of each currency after all deals, merchant and interbank. If the dealer has bought more than sold, the position is **overbought**; if sold more, **oversold**. Either leaves the bank exposed to **exchange rate** movements, so the dealer must keep it within the limits management sets.

Both positions include deals that are ready now and forwards that fall due later.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Overbought means long: the bank gains if the currency rises and loses if it falls. Oversold means short: the opposite.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Overbought by USD 1 million (long). A fall in the dollar causes a loss on the net position.

items.title: Five dials that set an option's price
items.core_explanation_md:
An option's premium is not guessed; it comes from five inputs, and it helps to think of them as dials.

1. **Spot rate today**: where the currency trades now, which sets how far the strike is from the market.
2. **Time to maturity**: how long the holder has for the right to become valuable.
3. **Forward rate for that maturity**: where the market expects the rate for the same date.
4. **Interest rates** in the two currencies over the period, which drive the gap between spot and forward.
5. **Volatility**: how widely the rate is likely to swing between spot and forward.

The first four position the strike against where the rate is likely to be; the fifth says how far it may wander. Remember that every option also has three price elements you pay or fix: the strike, the premium and the spot rate at purchase.

items.title: Why a bank rents someone else's branch abroad
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank that wants to serve clients across borders has two choices: build branches in each country, or ask a local bank to act for it. **Correspondent banking** is the second choice.

- The local bank abroad, which carries out the work, is the **correspondent bank**.
- The bank back home that relies on it as its agent is the **respondent bank**.

Why do banks choose this route?

1. A branch network is expensive to build and run.
2. Some countries restrict foreign bank licences, so a branch may simply not be allowed.
3. The correspondent already has local staff, systems and standing, and charges fees for what it does.

In a narrow sense the two banks hold accounts with each other; in a wider sense, one bank can act as agent for another without any account between them.

items.title: Which correspondent services need an account behind them?

**No, a relationship and a credit assessment are enough:**

- buyer's credit and supplier's credit, bankers acceptances, guarantees
- foreign exchange services, including derivatives
- custody, trade referrals, credit reports on foreign parties

items.title: Nostro, Vostro, Loro: whose books are you reading?
items.core_explanation_md:
One account, three names. The name depends on **who is speaking**.

- **Nostro**: "our account with you". Said by the bank that owns the balance, about the foreign currency account it holds abroad.
- **Vostro**: "your account with us". Said by the bank that holds the account for someone else, about that other bank's account kept in its books in the home currency.
- **Loro**: "their account with them". Said by a third bank, about an account two other banks have between them.

For the same account: the owner calls it Nostro, the holder calls it Vostro, and an outsider calls it Loro.

A **mirror account** is different: it is not an account with anyone. It is the owner's own bookkeeping copy of its Nostro, kept in the foreign currency and the home currency, so that entries can be matched with the statement the correspondent sends.

items.title: Messages versus money: telling the payment rails apart
items.core_explanation_md:
Two jobs are easy to confuse: **sending the instruction** and **settling the money**.

- **SWIFT** carries the secure message. It is a co-operative owned by its member banks and institutions, and it authenticates messages through keys the banks exchange with each other. It is not itself a place where funds are settled.
- **CHIPS** (New York, US dollars) nets participants' instructions through the day; each bank's net position is then debited or credited to its account with the Federal Reserve. It is mainly used for interbank foreign exchange and Eurodollar settlements.
- **Fedwire** (run by the Federal Reserve) settles payments one by one, on a gross basis. Banks are identified by ABA numbers.
- **CHAPS** is the British counterpart to CHIPS, handling payments in London.
- **TARGET** (today TARGET2) is the euro real-time gross settlement system.

A useful habit: ask of any system, *does it only message, or does it settle, and if it settles, net or gross?*

items.title: RTGS: large payments, settled one by one
items.core_explanation_md:
**RTGS** (Real Time Gross Settlement) is the Reserve Bank's system for large-value rupee transfers between banks.

Read the name word by word:
- **Real time**: an instruction is processed the moment it arrives.
- **Gross**: every payment is settled on its own, never netted against another.
- **Settlement**: it happens in the books of the Reserve Bank, so banks move funds through their accounts with it, and a settled payment is **final and irrevocable**.

Three facts to remember for the exam:
1. **Floor**: ₹2,00,000 is the minimum for a single remittance.
2. **Ceiling**: none set by RBI.
3. **Hours**: every day, around the clock (24x7x365), since 14 December 2020.

items.title: NEFT: batches every half hour, round the clock
items.core_explanation_md:
**NEFT** (National Electronic Funds Transfer) is a centralised system owned and run by the Reserve Bank. Unlike RTGS it does not settle each payment on arrival: payments are collected and settled in **batches at half-hourly intervals**, and it works every day of the year, around the clock.

- **Size of payment**: RBI sets no limit. A member bank may set its own limits, based on its risk view and with its Board's approval.
- **Credit to the beneficiary**: expected within two hours of the batch settlement.
- **Without an account**: a person with no bank account can send money by depositing cash at an NEFT-enabled branch, giving address and telephone details, but only up to ₹50,000 per transaction.

Contrast with RTGS: NEFT has no floor at ₹2,00,000 and settles in batches, RTGS settles one by one.

items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes CHAPS, the sterling system in London, as working like CHIPS on a **net** settlement principle.

The Bank of England, which operates CHAPS, describes it differently: payments between direct participants are settled **individually, on a gross basis**, in its real-time gross settlement system, and are irrevocable.

What to do with this:
- Treat CHAPS as the British high-value sterling system, with TARGET2 and Fedwire as the euro and dollar real-time gross systems.
- Do not rely on the net-versus-gross label for CHAPS alone. If an exam statement says CHAPS nets like CHIPS, it follows the courseware wording; the operator's own description is gross.
- CHIPS is the one of the group that nets.

items.title: NRI or PIO: who counts?
items.core_explanation_md:
Two labels decide who may open non-resident accounts, and both start with **residence outside India**.

- **NRI**: resident outside India **and** a citizen of India.
- **PIO**: resident outside India, a citizen of another country (not Bangladesh or Pakistan, unless the Government specifies otherwise), but with an Indian link: once an Indian citizen, born in a territory that joined India after 15 August 1947, a child, grandchild or great-grandchild of such a person, or the foreign-origin spouse of one. An **OCI cardholder** resident outside India is included.

So the quick test is: *which passport, and where do you live?* An Indian passport holder living abroad is an NRI. A foreign passport holder with Indian roots is a PIO. An Indian citizen on a short trip abroad is still a resident of India.

items.title: NRE or NRO: where does the money come from, and can it leave?
items.core_explanation_md:
Both are rupee accounts. What separates them is the **character of the money**.

- **NRE** holds money that came from abroad (and its interest). It is **fully repatriable**, and interest is exempt from income tax. Open only to NRIs and PIOs.
- **NRO** holds money earned or due in India: legitimate dues, transfers from other NRO accounts, and rupee gifts or loans from a resident relative within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme. It is **not freely repatriable**: only current income can go out, plus balances up to **USD 1 million per financial year** for NRIs and PIOs. Its interest is taxable. Anyone resident outside India can open one.

A useful reflex: money that arrived from abroad goes to NRE; money that grew up in India stays in NRO. When a resident becomes a non-resident, the old resident account is re-designated as an NRO account.

items.title: The USD 1 million window out of an NRO account
items.core_explanation_md:
An NRO balance is not repatriable as such. The exception is a yearly allowance:

- **Who**: NRIs and PIOs.
- **How much**: up to **USD 1 million per financial year** (April to March), counted together with their other eligible assets.
- **Which transfers count**: remittances abroad *and* transfers to an NRE account sit inside the same allowance.
- **Conditions**: the conditions in the Remittance of Assets regulations, and tax paid or cleared.

The allowance **resets on 1 April**; it does not carry over. Money above the limit can be sent in a later financial year.

items.title: FCNR(B) and SNRR: the two specialist accounts
items.core_explanation_md:
**FCNR(B)**: a **foreign currency** term deposit. Held in a freely convertible currency, for **one to five years**, by NRIs and PIOs only. It is repatriable, and because the deposit is in foreign currency the depositor carries no exchange risk on the principal in that currency.

**SNRR**: a **business** rupee account for a person abroad who has a business interest in India. It carries the name of the business, earns **no interest**, runs only for the life of the contract or business, and is repatriable.

Contrast with NRO, which has no business purpose, no tenure limit, and is not freely repatriable.

items.title: Borrowing against a non-resident deposit
items.core_explanation_md:
A non-resident can raise a loan against a deposit instead of breaking it.

- **In India** (against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits): to the depositor or to a third party, at usual margin, with no overall ceiling. The funds may not be used for **relending, agricultural or plantation activity, or real estate investment**.
- **Third-party loans**: the depositor must receive **no foreign exchange consideration**, direct or indirect, for pledging the deposit.
- **Repayment of a loan to the depositor**: by adjusting the deposit, by inward remittance, or out of the depositor's NRO balance.
- **While the loan is live**, the deposit **cannot be withdrawn prematurely**.
- **Outside India**: the bank's foreign branches or correspondents may lend against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits, at usual margin; loans against **NRO** balances abroad are not permitted.

items.title: A housing loan for an NRI: who lends, how it is secured, how it is repaid
items.core_explanation_md:
An NRI or PIO may borrow rupees to buy a **home** in India from an authorised dealer bank or a housing finance institution approved by the National Housing Bank.

- **Terms**: the amount, margin and repayment period are the same as for a resident borrower.
- **Disbursal**: the loan may **not be credited to an NRE, FCNR(B) or NRNR account**.
- **Security**: **equitable mortgage** of the property, and a lien on other assets in India if necessary.
- **Repayment**: from abroad by remittance; from an NRE, FCNR(B), NRNR, NRO or NRSR account; from **rental income** from the property; or by a **relative in India** through an account-to-account transfer.
- **Rate**: must conform to RBI and NHB directions.

items.title: Two ways to invest: money that can leave, money that stays
items.core_explanation_md:
When an NRI invests in India, the first decision is the **route**, because it fixes where the money may go on exit.

**Repatriation route** (Schedule III, listed equity and mutual fund units)
- Pay by inward remittance, or from a **repatriable** deposit account. A designated repatriable rupee account is used only for these investments.
- Sale proceeds (net of taxes) may be **sent abroad** or kept in that designated account. For mutual fund units, the NRI chooses between remitting and any permitted account.

**Non-repatriation route** (Schedule IV: equity, units, LLP capital; also firms and proprietary concerns)
- Pay by remittance, or from an **NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO** account.
- Proceeds go **only to the NRO account**, whichever account paid. The amount invested and the gain **cannot be repatriated**.

Shortcut: *repatriable in, repatriable out; non-repatriable investments always come back to an NRO account.*

items.title: Shares on the stock exchange: what changed in June 2026
items.core_explanation_md:
Courseware written before mid-2026 describes the **Portfolio Investment Scheme**: only NRIs and PIOs, through a designated bank branch, up to 5% of a company's paid-up capital each and 10% for all NRIs together.

On **12 June 2026** the Government amended the Non-Debt Instruments Rules (S.O. 3030(E)), and on **15 June 2026** the Reserve Bank gave effect to it in A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 14:

- **Who**: every **individual person resident outside India**, not only NRIs and OCIs, may buy and sell shares of listed Indian companies on a recognised stock exchange on a repatriation basis.
- **Limits**: **enhanced** from the old 5% and 10%. The circular itself does not state the new figures.
- **Account**: the bank opens a repatriable rupee account for the investor.
- **Breach of limits**: the holding is reclassified from portfolio investment to direct investment under the framework for foreign portfolio investors.

For the exam, remember the **direction of change** (wider eligibility, higher limits). Do not quote the old 5% and 10% as current.

items.title: Buying and selling property in India as an NRI
items.core_explanation_md:
What an NRI or OCI may do with immovable property in India:

- **Buy**: residential or commercial property from a resident, NRI or OCI. **Not** agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property.
- **Receive as gift** (not agricultural): from a relative who is a resident, NRI or OCI. **Inherit**: any property, from anyone who acquired it lawfully.
- **Sell or gift**: non-agricultural property to a resident, NRI or OCI; **agricultural land only to a resident**.
- **Pay for it**: through banking channels, or from **NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO** accounts. Not by travellers' cheques or foreign currency notes.

Restricted buyers: citizens of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal, Bhutan, Macau, Hong Kong and North Korea need prior RBI permission (other than for a lease of up to five years), but this bar **does not apply to an OCI**.

items.title: Sending the sale proceeds of a property abroad
items.core_explanation_md:
Selling the property is easy; sending the money out has conditions. For non-agricultural property sold by an NRI or PIO:

items.title: Current or capital: does it change what you own abroad?
items.core_explanation_md:
FEMA sorts every foreign exchange transaction into two boxes. The test is one question: **does the transaction change the resident's assets or liabilities outside India?**

- **No change: current account.** Paying a child's tuition abroad, family maintenance, a holiday, medical treatment. Residents may buy or sell foreign exchange for these freely, except for the few purposes the Central Government has prohibited (lottery winnings, lottery tickets, racing income, banned magazines, football pools and sweepstakes).
- **A change: capital account.** Buying shares abroad creates an asset outside India; buying a property abroad does the same; opening a foreign bank account does too. These are allowed only as the rules permit and up to the limits they set.

The LRS is the window that lets a resident individual do **either kind, or both**, up to one annual ceiling.

items.title: The LRS in one view
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who**: any resident individual, **minors included** (the natural guardian countersigns). Not companies, firms, HUFs or trusts.

**How much**: up to **USD 2,50,000 per financial year** (April to March), for current account, capital account, or a mix.

**How often**: as often as you like. What counts is the **cumulative total** for the year from all sources in India.

**The one-way gate**: once USD 2,50,000 has been used, no more remittances under the scheme that year, **even if the money from your investments has come back to India**.

**Paperwork**: PAN for every transaction whatever the amount; the purpose is declared in **Form A2**; the bank is guided by that declaration, but the **remitter is ultimately responsible** for compliance. Any freely convertible currency may be remitted.

items.title: What the LRS will not pay for
items.core_explanation_md:
Some remittances are out of bounds even inside the USD 2,50,000 limit:

- anything **prohibited** (Schedule I) or **restricted** (Schedule II) in the current account rules, such as lottery tickets
- **margins or margin calls** to overseas exchanges or counterparties
- buying **FCCBs** issued by Indian companies in the overseas secondary market
- **trading in foreign exchange** abroad
- capital account remittances to countries the **FATF** has identified as non-cooperative
- remittances to individuals or entities flagged as posing **significant terrorism risk**
- **gifting in foreign currency** by one resident to another, for the credit of the latter's foreign currency account abroad

A simple way to remember the pattern: speculation on exchange or margin, anything illegal at home, and anything touching sanctioned or high-risk destinations.

items.title: Where the money may go: permitted purposes
items.core_explanation_md:
Within the annual limit, a resident individual may remit for:

- **Travel**: private visits to any country except **Nepal and Bhutan**; business trips, conferences, specialised training
- **People**: gifts or donations, maintenance of close relatives abroad, emigration, going abroad for employment
- **Health**: medical treatment, check-ups, or accompanying a patient
- **Education**: studies abroad
- **Anything else** that is a current account transaction not otherwise defined as one in FEMA, which the bank may process without RBI permission if it is not prohibited or restricted and is genuine

Capital account uses such as investing abroad or buying property abroad are also allowed within the same limit.

items.title: Capital account remittances: extra conditions
items.core_explanation_md:
Sending money abroad to **invest or hold assets** brings extra conditions that current account remittances do not carry:

- **Designate one branch** of an authorised dealer through which all capital account remittances go.
- **One-year relationship**: the account with that bank should be at least a year old; a new customer faces due diligence on the account and source of funds.
- **No borrowed money**: banks may not lend, fund-based or non-fund-based, to help a resident make a capital account remittance under the LRS. They may do so for current account remittances.
- **Bring back what is not used**: unspent or unused foreign exchange must be surrendered to an authorised person within **180 days** of receipt, realisation, purchase, acquisition or return to India, unless reinvested. Income earned on the investments may be retained and reinvested.
- **Foreign currency account**: no prior approval is needed to open one abroad. Banks in India cannot open foreign currency accounts for residents under the LRS.

items.title: Families and the sole proprietor: who shares the limit?
items.core_explanation_md:
Two situations often catch candidates out.

**Family members.** Each resident individual has **his or her own** USD 2,50,000. Remittances can be **consolidated** across family members, but for a capital account transaction (opening a bank account, investing), another family member's limit **cannot be clubbed in** unless that person is a **co-owner or co-partner** of the investment or account.

**The sole proprietor.** A sole proprietorship has **no legal existence apart from its owner**. If the proprietor remits USD 2,50,000 in his own name, the same proprietor cannot remit a second USD 2,50,000 by debiting the business's current account. The eligibility used is the **individual's**.

items.title: A rupee gift or loan to a close relative who is an NRI
items.core_explanation_md:
A resident can send rupees (not foreign currency) to a close relative who is an **NRI or PIO**.

**Gift**: by crossed cheque or electronic transfer; credited to the relative's **NRO account**; counted within the giver's USD 2,50,000.

**Loan**, all of these together:
- **interest-free**, **minimum one year**
- within the lender's USD 2,50,000
- used for the borrower's **personal needs or own business in India**, never for chit fund or Nidhi business, agricultural or plantation activity, real estate business, farm houses or TDR trading
- **credited to the NRO account**; **not remitted abroad**
- repaid by inward remittance, or by debit to an **NRO, NRE or FCNR** account, or from the sale proceeds of the asset against which the loan was granted

"Close relative" means a relative as defined in section 2(77) of the Companies Act, 2013.

items.title: TCS on foreign remittances: the three things to know
items.core_explanation_md:
When a resident individual sends money abroad under the LRS, the **authorised dealer bank collects tax at source (TCS)** from the remitter. Three facts decide it.

1. **The trigger**: the remittances in the financial year, taken together, **exceed ₹10 lakh**.
2. **The rate depends on the purpose**: **2%** for **education or medical treatment**; **20%** for **every other purpose** (investment abroad, gifts, family maintenance, travel and the rest).
3. **The collector**: the authorised dealer bank, at the time of the remittance.

The provision is section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026.

items.title: When no TCS is collected on an LRS remittance
items.core_explanation_md:
Three situations switch the collection off or move it to someone else.

- **Education funded by a loan** from a financial institution: **no TCS** on that remittance.
- **Overseas tour package**: the **seller** (the tour operator) collects **2%** on the package price, with no ₹10 lakh threshold. The bank does **not** collect again on the amount the seller has already taxed.
- **Tax already deducted**: if the person receiving the money is subject to tax deducted at source under another provision of the Act and it **has** been deducted, the bank does not collect TCS.

Check order for a bank officer: *tour package already taxed? education loan? tax already deducted? If none, test the ₹10 lakh aggregate.*

items.title: Old numbers in older books: what changed in 2026
items.core_explanation_md:
Courseware written in 2020 or soon after teaches the **original** TCS rules: **5%** on LRS remittances above **₹7 lakh**, **0.5%** for an education loan, and **10%** if PAN or Aadhaar is missing.

The current position for the December 2026 exam (section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025):

- Threshold: **₹10 lakh** a year, not ₹7 lakh.
- Education or medical treatment: **2%** (it was 5% until 1 April 2026).
- All other purposes: **20%**.
- Education loan from a financial institution: **no TCS** (not 0.5%).
- Overseas tour package: **2%** collected by the seller, with no threshold.

If an exam question quotes the older figures, it follows the older rules; the table above is the current law.

items.title: The LRS ceiling over the years: up, then down, then up again
items.core_explanation_md:
The limit has moved with the macro conditions, not in a straight line.

- **4 Feb 2004**: USD 25,000 (launch)
- **20 Dec 2006**: USD 50,000
- **8 May 2007**: USD 1,00,000
- **26 Sep 2007**: USD 2,00,000 (the first peak)
- **14 Aug 2013**: cut to **USD 75,000**
- **3 Jun 2014**: raised to USD 1,25,000
- **26 May 2015**: **USD 2,50,000**, the figure that still applies

Two things to remember: the limit has **fallen once** (2013), and today's USD 2,50,000 has applied **since 26 May 2015**, the date the current account facilities were folded into it.

items.title: Current account purposes sit inside the ceiling, with a few exits
items.core_explanation_md:
Every current account facility an individual uses (private visits, gifts or donations, going abroad for employment, emigration, maintenance of relatives, business trips, medical treatment, studies) counts against the **same USD 2,50,000**. Beyond it, **RBI permission** is needed, except where the direction itself provides a route.

- **Private visits**: the whole trip counts, including rail or road transport, passes and overseas hotels. A tour operator may collect in rupees or foreign currency.
- **Business trips**: if the **employer** pays, the spend is a residual current account transaction **outside** the LRS, and the bank may allow it **without limit** after checking bona fides.
- **Gift or donation** and **maintenance of relatives**: up to the ceiling, with no separate sub-limit.

items.title: The three purposes that can go beyond USD 2,50,000 without RBI
items.core_explanation_md:
Emigration, medical care and study abroad have their own routes above the ceiling.

**Emigration**: up to the amount the destination country **prescribes**, or the ceiling. Anything more is allowed only for **incidental expenses** in the new country, never to buy eligibility through bonds, land or a business there.

**Medical treatment**: up to the ceiling **without an estimate**. Above it, the bank may release exchange under general permission on an **estimate** from a doctor in India or a hospital or doctor abroad. A person who falls ill after leaving may also be released exchange **without RBI approval**. An **attendant** accompanying the patient gets up to USD 2,50,000 a year.

**Studies**: up to the ceiling **without a university estimate**. Above it, **without RBI approval**, on the institution's estimate.

items.title: The capital account routes, and the IFSC window
items.core_explanation_md:
An individual may use the LRS for capital account purposes in these routes:

- opening a **foreign currency account** abroad with a bank (no prior RBI approval needed)
- buying **immovable property abroad**
- **overseas direct investment** and **overseas portfolio investment**, under the Overseas Investment Rules, Regulations and Directions of **2022**
- **loans** (including in rupees) to **NRI relatives**

Other permitted uses: **objects of art** (subject to the Foreign Trade Policy), and a **demand draft** in your own or the beneficiary's name against a self-declaration.

**IFSC window**: banks may facilitate remittances to an **International Financial Services Centre in India** for financial products there, or for transactions elsewhere through a foreign currency account held in the IFSC. You may open that account, but you may **not settle domestic transactions** with other residents through it.

items.title: What the bank must do on every LRS remittance
items.core_explanation_md:
The authorised dealer carries real duties.

1. **Funds**: the money must come from the **remitter's own account or instrument** (cheque on the applicant's account, debit, demand draft or pay order, or the cardholder's card).
2. **Certify** that the remittance is not made directly or indirectly **by or to ineligible entities**.
3. **Know the customer**: KYC and anti-money laundering rules apply; for a **new customer's capital account** remittance, carry out **due diligence** and get the **previous year's bank statement** or the latest tax assessment order or return.
4. **Keep records** of the information on which the transaction was done.
5. **Refuse in writing** if the applicant will not comply, and **report to RBI** if contravention or evasion is suspected.
6. **Report** the remittance through **FETERS**, following the Master Direction on reporting under FEMA.

Also: a bank may not market foreign currency deposit schemes of overseas branches, or act as agent for overseas mutual funds, in India without **prior RBI approval**.

items.title: Why a seller trusts a bank instead of a stranger
items.core_explanation_md:
A seller in one country and a buyer in another do not know each other. The **documentary credit** closes the gap: the **buyer's bank** promises to pay the seller **if** the seller presents the **documents** the credit asks for, within the time stated, and complying with every term.

Two ideas run through the whole subject:
- The banks deal in **documents, not goods**. They pay or refuse on what the papers say, not on what is in the container.
- The credit is **separate from the sales contract**. A dispute about the goods does not change what the bank must do on conforming documents.

The rules that make this work are written by the **International Chamber of Commerce** (founded 1919, Paris). The set is the **UCPDC**, first issued in 1933 and revised in 1951, 1962, 1974, 1983, 1993 and **2007**. Today's edition is **UCP 600**, effective **1 July 2007**.

items.title: What each revision added: a memory ladder
items.core_explanation_md:
A short ladder helps recall which version brought which idea.

- **1951**: the word **applicant**; the settlement methods; **banks deal in documents, not goods**.
- **1962**: the credit is **separate from the sales contract**; a confirming bank negotiates **without recourse**.
- **1974**: **nomination**.
- **1983**: duty of **reasonable care on authenticity**; **deferred payment**; definition of **transhipment**.
- **1993 (UCP 500)**: a credit is **irrevocable if silent**; **reasonable time not exceeding 7 banking days** to examine documents; **non-documentary conditions disregarded**.
- **2007 (UCP 600)**: articles on **definitions** and **interpretations**; **no more revocable credits**; examination in a maximum of **5 banking days following the day of presentation**.

The move from **7** days to **5** days between UCP 500 and UCP 600 is a favourite exam point.

items.title: Seven parties, one question each
items.core_explanation_md:
Ask of every party: **whom does it act for, and what does it do?**

- **Applicant** (the buyer/importer): asks for the credit to be opened.
- **Issuing (opening) bank**: the applicant's bank, which **establishes** the credit and carries the primary payment promise.
- **Beneficiary** (the seller/exporter): gets paid if the documents comply.
- **Advising bank**: in the seller's country, acts as the issuing bank's **agent**, **authenticates** the credit and tells the beneficiary.
- **Confirming bank**: adds **its own** undertaking to pay, standing beside the issuing bank.
- **Nominated (negotiating) bank**: **negotiates** the documents and pays the beneficiary.
- **Reimbursing bank**: **reimburses** the negotiating or confirming bank.

One bank can wear several hats. The advising, confirming and negotiating banks may all be the same bank.

items.title: Irrevocable, confirmed, transferable: three words, three different protections
items.core_explanation_md:
**Irrevocable**: cannot be changed or cancelled unless **all** parties agree, the opener, the beneficiary and any confirming bank. Under UCP 600 credits are **irrevocable** unless they say otherwise, and the earlier idea of a **revocable** credit was removed in 2007.

**Confirmed**: a **second bank** (usually in the exporter's country) adds its **own** undertaking. It steps into the issuing bank's shoes. It is **not obliged to confirm later amendments**, and must tell the beneficiary if it will not.

**Transferable**: the credit must **say so**. It can pass in whole or in part to one or more **second beneficiaries**, but a second beneficiary **cannot transfer it again**.

The three answer different worries: **changes** (irrevocable), **the issuing bank's credit risk or country risk** (confirmed) and **the beneficiary is a middleman** (transferable).

items.title: Paying for goods before they ship, and paying later: the special credits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Advance before shipment**
- **Red clause**: the beneficiary can draw an **advance** against a written undertaking to deliver the transport documents later.
- **Green clause**: the same, but the advance also needs a **document showing the goods are warehoused**, so it is a little safer for the bank.

**When the money moves**
- **Sight**: paid when conforming documents are presented.
- **Usance (acceptance)**: a **draft** is drawn payable at a future date, counted from a stated point such as the shipment date or the draft date.
- **Deferred payment**: **no draft**; the due date is simply stated in the credit.
- **Negotiation**: the nominated bank **gives value** for the documents or draft.

**Credits that sit on other credits**
- **Back-to-back**: a middleman uses an export credit to support a **local supplier credit**.
- **Revolving**: covers **consecutive instalments** of a delivery contract; the second instalment is not effective until the first is paid.

items.title: The standby credit: a promise that is hoped never to be used
items.core_explanation_md:
A **standby letter of credit** looks like a credit but behaves like a **guarantee**. It is a safeguard against **default**, not a payment instrument.

- If the customer fails to pay or perform, the beneficiary **claims** by presenting a **declaration** (with whatever other documents the standby asks for) that the customer failed.
- It is governed by **UCP** or by the **International Standby Practices, ISP 98**.

Compare with a **documentary credit**: there, the seller expects to use it on every shipment. With a standby, the happy ending is that it **expires unused**.

items.title: UCP 600 as a map: 39 articles in nine groups
items.core_explanation_md:
UCP 600 trimmed the rulebook from **49 articles to 39**. A map of the groups is more useful than memorising numbers.

- **1-5**: definitions, interpretations, and that the credit is **independent** of the underlying contract
- **6-10**: availability, expiry, what the **issuing** and **confirming** banks undertake, **advising**, **amendments**
- **11-17**: pre-advised credits, **nominated bank**, **reimbursement**, **complying presentation**, **original documents**
- **18**: commercial **invoice**
- **19-27**: **transport** documents
- **28**: **insurance** documents
- **29-33**: extension of expiry, **tolerance**, partial and instalment drawings, hours of presentation
- **34-37**: **disclaimers** (what banks are not responsible for)
- **38-39**: **transferability** and **assignment of proceeds**

Two more facts: UCP 600 applies **only if the credit says it is subject to it** (and parties may exclude parts if stated), and **DOCDEX** is the ICC's dispute resolution route for credit disputes.

items.title: Irrevocable by default, and how an amendment gets accepted
items.core_explanation_md:
**Irrevocable by default.** UCP 600 defines a credit as irrevocable. A credit is irrevocable even if it does not say so (Article 3), and the old notion of a **revocable** credit disappeared in 2007. A prudent seller still asks in the sales contract for an **irrevocable** credit.

**Amendments.** A credit cannot be amended or cancelled without the agreement of the **issuing bank**, the **confirming bank** (if any) and the **beneficiary** (Article 10).

What if the beneficiary says nothing? If it presents documents that comply with the credit **and** with any amendment it has **not yet accepted**, that presentation is **deemed to be notice of acceptance** of the amendment, and from that moment the credit is amended.

So silence is not acceptance, but **acting on the amendment is**.

items.title: Examining documents: five banking days and what to do with a discrepancy
items.core_explanation_md:
**The clock.** A bank has up to **five banking days following the day of presentation** to decide whether to honour or refuse. (UCP 500 gave a reasonable time of up to seven.) A **banking day** is a day on which the bank is **regularly open** where the act is to be done.

**The presentation period.** Documents must usually be presented within **21 days** of shipment, but this applies to **original transport documents**. If no transport document is required, the credit should state its own period.

**What counts as a discrepancy.** Data need **not be identical** across documents, but must **not conflict**. **Non-documentary conditions** (conditions not tied to a required document) are **disregarded**.

**When a bank refuses**, it can: hold the documents pending the presenter's instructions; hold them until the **applicant waives** the discrepancy and the bank agrees to accept; return them; or act on instructions previously given. There is **no payment under reserve or indemnity**.

items.title: Who owes what: a duty ledger for each party
items.core_explanation_md:
| Party | Core duty |
| --- | --- |
| **Applicant** | Gives **complete, precise** instructions; avoids **excessive detail**; **indemnifies** banks against obligations imposed by **foreign laws**; pays charges that a third party does not |
| **Issuing bank** | Assures itself of the applicant's **creditworthiness**; gives a **definite undertaking**; examines documents with **reasonable care**; refuses within **five banking days** and says whether documents are **held** or **returned** |
| **Advising bank** | May choose whether to advise; if it does, checks **authenticity** with reasonable care; if unable to, tells the **issuing bank and the beneficiary** |
| **Confirming bank** | Adds its **own** undertaking; if it will not confirm, tells the issuing bank **without delay** |
| **Negotiating bank** | Negotiates only if documents **appear on their face** to comply |
| **Reimbursing bank** | Reimburses on the issuing bank's **authorisation**, under **URR 725** |
| **Beneficiary** | Cannot rely on the contract **between the banks** or between the applicant and the issuing bank |

items.title: What banks do not answer for
items.core_explanation_md:
UCP 600 keeps banks out of problems they cannot control. A bank does **not** take responsibility for:

- the **genuineness** of the documents (it examines them on their face)
- **delay or loss** of messages or documents in transmission
- **errors in translating or interpreting** technical terms
- **interruption of business** by acts of God, riots, civil commotion and similar causes (so a credit that **expires during a force majeure** is **not** honoured later)
- the **acts of correspondent banks**, whether the applicant or the bank chose them

And the applicant is liable for **charges** a third party does not pay, and for losses arising from **foreign laws**.

The common thread: banks answer for **reasonable examination**, not for outcomes that depend on the world outside the documents.

items.title: Smaller changes that UCP 600 made, and the reasons for them
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Deferred payment and acceptance** (Arts 7, 8, 12(b)): the issuing and confirming banks must **reimburse the nominated bank at maturity**, even if it prepaid or purchased early.
- **Advising** (Art 9(b)): the advising bank certifies that its advice **reflects the credit it received**, and so does any **second** advising bank.
- **Original documents** (Art 17): a document is original if it **looks** original, for example bears an apparently original signature, mark, stamp or label, or says it is original.
- **Transport**: a **charter party** bill of lading may be signed by the **charterer**; transport documents **no longer need the word "clean"**.
- **Insurance** (Art 28): **wider** cover than asked is acceptable; the stated percentage is a **minimum**; an **exclusion clause** may be mentioned.
- **Lost in transit** (Art 35): if the nominated bank has determined the presentation complies and forwarded the documents, the issuing bank must **honour or reimburse** even if they are lost on the way.
- **Transferable credits** (Art 38): a **second beneficiary** presents to the **transferring bank**.

items.title: The draft and the invoice: what a checker looks for
items.core_explanation_md:
**Draft (bill of exchange)**
- drawn by the **beneficiary** on the **issuing bank**
- payable at the **tenor** the credit states (sight or a stated period)

- in the **currency of the credit**, for an amount **not above** it
- any **correction** authenticated by the drawer

**Commercial invoice**
- made out by the **beneficiary**, normally in the **applicant's name**
- goods described **exactly as in the credit**
- shows the **order or contract number** and the **credit number**
- **value not above the credit amount**
- states the **terms of sale** (FOB, C&F, CIF) and shipping particulars

items.title: The bill of lading, line by line
items.core_explanation_md:
The bill of lading is the **receipt** from the carrier that the goods were shipped on a named vessel on a stated date. A checker confirms:

1. **Full set** of negotiable originals, as the credit requires.
2. **Signed** by the shipowner or its authorised agent.
3. **Goods description** matches the credit and the invoice.
4. **Credit number** and **issuing bank** shown.
5. **Freight** shown as paid or to pay, as the credit requires.
6. **"Shipped on board"** wording if the credit asks.
7. **Consignee**: to the **order of the shipper**, blank endorsed or endorsed to the issuing bank, as the credit says.
8. **Shipment date** inside the shipment period.
9. **Partial shipment or transhipment** noted if allowed.
10. **Not claused**, unless claused bills are allowed.

items.title: After the bank pays: proof that the goods actually arrived
items.core_explanation_md:
When a bank remits foreign exchange for an import, the Reserve Bank expects **evidence that the goods came in**. For **every import**, whatever the value, the authorised dealer must make sure the importer provides it.

- **Normal imports**: the **bill of entry number, port code and date**, which the bank uses to mark evidence of import in the **IDPMS** (the import data system).
- **By post**: a **customs assessment certificate** or **postal appraisal form**; **by courier**: the **courier bill of entry**.
- **Bonded or special zones**: the **ex-bond bill of entry** or similar document.
- **Delivery against acceptance**: the bank checks the evidence in **IDPMS when it remits**. If the importer genuinely cannot show it (for example the goods are delayed), the bank may allow **reasonable time of up to three months from the date of remittance**.
- The bank creates an **Outward Remittance Message (ORM)** for every remittance.

Watch the date: RBI issued new consolidated directions on **16 January 2026**, in force from **1 October 2026**, that supersede the Import Master Direction.

items.title: Safeguards when a bank opens credits for importers
items.core_explanation_md:
The bank issuing a credit is on the hook for the importer. The safeguards are mostly about **knowing the customer and the supplier**.

- **Know the importer**: clear internal guidelines, due diligence and KYC, a track record; extra care on **large-value** deals or a **sudden jump in business**, and even where the importer offers **100% cash margin**.
- **Know the supplier**: a **credit report on the overseas seller**. When the bank takes documents directly from the supplier, the report may be skipped only where the invoice is **USD 300,000 or less** and the bank is satisfied about the transaction and the importer.
- **Know the rules**: exchange control, trade control, licences, delegated powers.
- **Follow up**: evidence of import; for a **sight bill** the importer does not retire, **take possession of the goods and keep insurance running**.
- **Usance credits**: only for **reputed clients** with **adequate security**, because the goods are delivered on acceptance.

items.title: Risks in credit transactions, seen from each side
items.core_explanation_md:
**What can go wrong for everyone**: documents **rejected for discrepancies**; local law that **conflicts** with the rules; **embargoes** or **currency restrictions**; a **court order** stopping payment even after acceptance; the buyer refusing to take up documents until the **goods arrive**; **disputes over quality** after the documents are accepted.

**For the bank**: open credits only for **regular customers**; call for bills of lading **in the bank's name**; no credits for **restricted-list goods**, and obtain the **import licence** where one is needed; apply the same checks as for **fund-based** limits even if cash margin is offered; **hedge large transactions** by a forward contract.

**For the buyer**: check the seller's **creditworthiness**; put **safety clauses** in the credit; know the **seller's country's** export rules.

**For the seller**: prepare documents **exactly** as the credit asks, so the issuing bank has **nothing to point to**.

items.title: URR 725: how a negotiating bank gets repaid by a third bank
items.core_explanation_md:
When a credit says the negotiating bank may claim its money from **another bank**, that other bank is the **reimbursing bank**. The ICC's **URR 725** sets out how this works.

Three roles:
- **Issuing bank**: issued the credit and **authorised** the reimbursement.
- **Reimbursing bank**: accepted that authorisation and **pays the claim**.
- **Claiming bank**: **paid or committed** under the credit and **presents the claim**.

Three principles:
1. The reimbursement authorisation should say it is **subject to URR 725**.
2. The **reimbursing bank is bound** by the rules once it accepts, but the **claiming bank is not a party** to them: the arrangement is between the **issuing bank and the reimbursing bank** only.
3. The authorisation is **independent of the credit**: the reimbursing bank is **not concerned with or bound by** the credit's terms.

citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: What a valid reimbursement authority looks like
items.core_explanation_md:
The issuing bank must make the authority **clean and independent**:

- It **states** that it is subject to **URR 725**.
- It gives the **credit number**, the **currency and amount**, any **additional amount and tolerance**, the **claiming bank's name**, and who bears the **charges**.
- It is sent by **authenticated tele-transmission** with **no mail confirmation**.
- It is **precise and complete**, and does **not** carry a copy of the credit.

And the issuing bank **must not**:
- ask the claiming bank for a **certificate of compliance**
- put an **expiry date** on the reimbursement authority

The **reimbursing bank** is **not obliged** to honour a claim unless it has given a **reimbursement undertaking**.

items.title: Changing, claiming, refusing: the rules of the reimbursement path
items.core_explanation_md:
**Changing**: the issuing bank may **cancel or amend** an authorisation at any time by notice, **unless** the reimbursing bank has given an **undertaking**. An **irrevocable** authorisation needs the **reimbursing bank's agreement** to change. The reimbursing bank can **accept or reject** any amendment. An **undertaking** cannot be cancelled or amended without the **claiming bank's agreement**.

**Claiming**: by **tele-transmission** unless the issuing bank forbids it, with a **time draft** if one is required. Do not claim **more than 10 days before the due date**.

**Processing**: the reimbursing bank has a **reasonable time, not exceeding three banking days**. If it will not pay, it must tell the **claiming bank and the issuing bank** quickly, preferably by tele-transmission.

items.title: Who bears what in the reimbursement chain
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Disputes about loss** (lost interest, exchange movements, charges) caused by the reimbursing bank not doing what it should are settled **between the claiming bank and the reimbursing bank**.
- **The reimbursing bank's charges** are normally for the **issuing bank**. If a third party is to pay, the issuing bank must say so in the credit and the authorisation.
- **The issuing bank indemnifies** the reimbursing bank against obligations imposed by **foreign laws and usages**.
- **The reimbursing bank is not responsible** for delay or loss in transit, interrupted business, acts of God, riots, wars, strikes or lockouts.

A useful way to remember it: the **issuing bank stands behind** the reimbursing bank; the **claiming bank must look to the reimbursing bank** for its own losses.

items.title: ISBP: the practice guide that sits beside UCP 600
items.core_explanation_md:
**UCP 600** gives the rules. **ISBP** shows how bankers **apply** them when they check documents.

- It is an **ICC publication**, a **companion** to UCP 600.
- It **cannot change** UCP 600; it explains standard practice within it.
- **History**: approved in **2002** as a companion to UCP 500; updated as **ICC publication 681** after UCP 600 (2007); fully revised as **ICC publication 745** in **July 2013**, adding new interpretations and points drawn from ICC official opinions.
- **Aims**: **uniform practice worldwide**, **fewer credits rejected** for discrepancies, and practices that **reduce discrepant presentations**.

A note on currency: the ICC has since issued a later edition, **ISBP 821 (July 2023)**. The syllabus names **ISBP 745**, so this course teaches that edition and flags the newer one.

items.title: Incoterms 2020: eleven rules in two families
items.core_explanation_md:
**Incoterms** are ICC rules for the **contract of sale** (not the contract of carriage). They say who arranges and pays for carriage, insurance and customs, and **where risk passes**.

**Seven rules for any mode of transport**
- **EXW** Ex Works
- **FCA** Free Carrier
- **CPT** Carriage Paid To
- **CIP** Carriage and Insurance Paid To
- **DAP** Delivered at Place
- **DPU** Delivered at Place **Unloaded**
- **DDP** Delivered Duty Paid

**Four rules for sea and inland waterway only**
- **FAS** Free Alongside Ship
- **FOB** Free on Board
- **CFR** Cost and Freight
- **CIF** Cost, Insurance and Freight

In force since **1 January 2020**. **DPU replaced DAT**, and under DPU the seller **unloads** the goods at destination (under DAP the seller does not).

items.title: Who carries what: the ladder from EXW to DDP
items.core_explanation_md:
Read the rules as a ladder. **Each step towards DDP moves another job from buyer to seller.**

- **EXW**: the buyer takes almost everything, even **loading** the goods.
- **FAS, FCA, FOB**: the seller delivers to the **carrier or the ship**, so **loading at origin** and **origin charges** are the seller's.
- **CFR, CIF, CPT, CIP**: the seller also pays the **main carriage** (ocean or air freight). (CIF and CIP add **insurance**.)
- **DPU**: the seller also bears **destination port charges** and **unloads**.
- **DDP**: the seller also does **customs clearance and pays duties**, the maximum responsibility.

Wherever you are on the ladder, **warehouse services and export packing** are the seller's. **Customs clearance and duties** are the buyer's except under **DDP**.

items.title: What changed between Incoterms 2010 and 2020
items.core_explanation_md:
- **FCA**: the buyer can instruct its carrier to issue a **bill of lading with an on-board notation** to the seller, so the seller can present it to its bank for **financing**.
- **Own transport**: FCA, DAP, DPU and DDP let buyer or seller use **its own vehicles**, not only a third-party carrier.
- **CIP**: insurance by default is now **Institute Cargo Clauses (A)**, **all risks**, in place of the old limited cover (Clauses C).
- **DPU** replaces **DAT**, and is the **only rule under which the seller unloads** at destination.
- **Costs** tied to carrier charges are set out more clearly.
- **Security** obligations (for example **screening of containers**) are addressed.

Check each term's year in a credit or contract: parties may agree to use an earlier edition if they name it.

items.title: Case file 1: the credit does not care about the contract
items.core_explanation_md:
**Scenario.** An importer opens a credit for machinery. The invoice matches the credit, but the importer then says the goods are not what the sales contract promised, and asks the bank to refuse payment.

**Answer.** The bank deals in **documents, not goods**, and the credit is **separate from the sale contract**. If the documents **comply**, the issuing bank must **honour** them. A dispute over the contract is for the buyer and seller, not a reason for the bank to refuse.

Two further points the courseware draws out:
- A **court order** may stop the bank paying, and the bank must then wait; **recovering** money from the applicant is a separate matter of **credit risk**, and should not be linked to honouring the credit.
- A bank must not itself **excuse a payment** by pointing to quality or contract disputes.

items.title: Case file 2: dates, partial shipments and insurance
items.core_explanation_md:
**Dates on documents.** A document may be **dated before the credit** was issued, as long as it is **not dated after the expiry date for presentation**, unless the credit says otherwise. The bank should not reject a document merely for pre-dating the credit.

**Partial shipment.** If the credit forbids it, but the goods go on **one vessel on one voyage** under **two bills of lading** with different dates, that is **not** a partial shipment. More than one set of transport documents for the **same means of transport and journey** is not partial even with different dates.

**Insurance.** If the credit is silent, cover must be **at least 110%** of the invoice value. The policy must not be dated **after the transport document**, **unless** it shows cover **from the date of shipment**.

items.title: Case file 3: the refusal clock, banking days and the closed-bank rule
items.core_explanation_md:
**Refusal clock.** The issuing bank must give notice of refusal and the discrepancies by the **close of the fifth banking day after the day it received the documents**. **Saturdays, Sundays and bank holidays are not banking days**, so a refusal sent on the next working Monday after a weekend may still be on time.

**Closed-bank rule.** If the **last day for presentation** falls on a day the bank is **closed**, it is extended to the **next banking day**. If banks in that place are **open** that day, there is **no extension**.

**Advising failure.** If an advising bank cannot advise a credit, it must tell the issuing bank **at once**. The issuing bank is **not responsible** for the advising bank's failure, even though it chose that bank.

items.title: Two sets of rules for every export: exchange control and trade control
items.core_explanation_md:
An exporter answers to two regulators for different things.

- **Trade control** (what may be exported, how, with which incentives): the **Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)**, under the Ministry of Commerce, through the **Foreign Trade Policy**.
- **Exchange control** (how the foreign money comes back): the **Reserve Bank of India**, under **FEMA**. Authorised dealer banks carry it out.

The key that opens both is the **Importer-Exporter Code (IEC)** from the DGFT, quoted in every declaration and form. Exporters of **services** also register with the **Services Export Promotion Council** or the **Federation of Indian Export Organisations**, and exporters of **software** with the **Software Technology Park of India**.

items.title: EDF, SOFTEX and the two clocks an exporter lives by
items.core_explanation_md:
**What is declared**: goods go on the **Export Declaration Form (EDF)**; software sent in non-physical form goes on the **SOFTEX** form. A few cases are **exempt** from declaring (listed in Regulation 4 of the Export Regulations), but the exporter must still **realise and repatriate the proceeds**.

**Clock 1: submit documents within 21 days** of the export. If late, the authorised dealer may still handle them **without prior RBI approval** if it is satisfied with the reasons.

**Clock 2: realise the money within nine months** of the export, for all exporters including SEZ units, status holders, EOUs and units in EHTPs, STPs and BTPs.
- **Warehouse abroad**: proceeds within **fifteen months** of shipment.
- **Bharat Mart**: **nine months** from the date of sale of the goods from the warehouse.

The period went to **fifteen months** in November 2025 and was **restored to nine months** on 5 June 2026, so **nine months** applies at the exam cut-off.

items.title: When the money is late: extending the realisation period
items.core_explanation_md:
The exporter applies to the authorised dealer. The bank may extend by **up to six months at a time**, whatever the invoice value, if **all** of these hold:

1. The exports are **not under investigation** by the Directorate of Enforcement, the CBI or other agencies.
2. The bank is satisfied the delay is for **reasons beyond the exporter's control**.
3. The exporter **declares** the proceeds will be realised in the extended period.
4. If the extension goes **beyond one year** from export, the exporter's **total outstanding** is within **USD 1 million or 10% of average export realisation in the last three financial years, whichever is higher**.

If the exporter has **sued the buyer abroad**, extension may be given **whatever the amount**. Cases outside these rules need **prior RBI Regional Office approval**. Every extension is **reported in EDPMS**.

items.title: Commission, refunds and advances: what the bank checks

**Refund of export proceeds**: allowed through the bank that realised them, for goods **re-imported for poor quality**, after due diligence, the bank checking that **no export incentive** was availed or it has been **surrendered**. Re-import need not be insisted on where the goods were **auctioned or destroyed** by the authorities.

**Advance from the buyer**: **ship within three years**, interest **not above the benchmark rate plus 100 basis points**, and the **documents routed through the bank that received the advance**.

items.title: Settling with neighbours: the Asian Clearing Union and the exceptions
items.core_explanation_md:
The **Asian Clearing Union (ACU)** lets member countries settle eligible payments in **ACU Dollar**, **ACU Euro** or **ACU Japanese Yen**, each equal in value to **one US dollar, euro or yen**. Banks keep these accounts with correspondents in other member countries.

Exceptions to remember:
- **Myanmar**: any freely convertible currency **in addition to** the ACU mechanism.
- **Iran** and **Sri Lanka**: eligible current account transactions, including trade, may be settled in **any permitted currency outside the ACU mechanism**.

Older books list the whole ACU group without the Sri Lanka relaxation. The Reserve Bank's current Master Direction is the authority.

items.title: Giving up on an export bill: the write-off limits and gates
items.core_explanation_md:
When an overseas buyer will not or cannot pay, an exporter can **write off** the unrealised bill, subject to limits.

**How much (a share of export proceeds realised in the preceding calendar year)**
- **Self-write-off**: **5%**, or **10%** for a **status holder**.
- **Write-off by the authorised dealer**: **10%**.
- The limits are **cumulative**.

**The gates**: outstanding for **more than a year**; **evidence of every effort** to collect; a **regular customer** for **six months** and KYC compliant; **proportionate export incentives surrendered**; a **chartered accountant's certificate** for self-write-off.

**Which cases qualify**: buyer **insolvent** (liquidator's certificate), **settled through an embassy or chamber of commerce**, goods **auctioned or destroyed** by authorities, buyer **untraceable**, an **undrawn balance** up to 10% of invoice value, legal action **out of proportion**, or a bill for a **letter-of-credit difference** that was dishonoured. For insolvency, settlement through an embassy or chamber, and goods auctioned or destroyed, the bank may write off **without limit**.

**Does not qualify**: exports to countries with **externalisation problems**, bills under **investigation** by the ED, DRI or CBI, or the subject of a **civil or criminal suit**. Write-offs are **reported in EDPMS**.

items.title: Netting a customer's exports against its imports: the set-off rules
items.core_explanation_md:
An exporter who is also an importer with the **same overseas party** may ask its bank to **set off** what it is owed against what it owes, instead of two payments crossing the world.

**Allowed**: with the **same overseas buyer/supplier**, or with **group or associate companies** through a centralised settlement arrangement.

**Conditions to check**
- **One authorised dealer** operates and supervises the arrangement.
- **No KYC, AML or CFT** concerns; transactions **not under investigation**.
- **ACU country** transactions stay **outside** it.
- **Goods against goods, services against services**: never goods against services.
- Both amounts **outstanding at the time**, and the export and import legs in the **same calendar year**.
- A **verifiable agreement** (a **written, enforceable** one for group settlement).
- **No tax avoidance**.
- Each transaction **reported separately, gross**.

The courseware adds: the **EDF is released only after the entire export proceeds have been adjusted**.

items.title: Keeping foreign exchange earned: EEFC, trade-fair and diamond accounts
items.core_explanation_md:
**EEFC account** (Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency)
- Only a **non-interest-bearing current account** with an authorised dealer.
- **100%** of foreign exchange earnings may be credited.
- Accruals in a calendar month must be **converted to rupees by the last day of the next month**, after approved uses and forward commitments.
- It is for **saving conversion costs**, not for **holding foreign currency assets**.
- **No credit**, fund-based or non-fund-based, against EEFC balances.
- A resident individual may add a **resident close relative** as joint holder (**former or survivor**).

**Trade fair account**: a **temporary** foreign currency account abroad; repatriate the balance **within one month** of the fair closing.

**Diamond Dollar Account**: for firms dealing in **diamonds and jewellery** with **three years' track record** and **average annual turnover of ₹3 crore** or more; **up to five** accounts.

items.title: Sending goods free of cost: the EDF waiver
items.core_explanation_md:
Normally every export needs an EDF. For **free-of-cost exports for export promotion**, a **status holder** can use an **EDF waiver** up to a yearly limit based on **average annual export realisation over the preceding three licensing years**:

- **2%** for most exporters.
- **Gems and jewellery, and articles of gold and precious metals**: **₹1 crore or 2%, whichever is lower**.
- **Pharmaceuticals, vaccines and life-saving drugs for health programmes of international agencies** (such as UN agencies, WHO-PAHO): up to **8%**.

Such free-of-cost supplies get **no duty drawback or other incentive**. Exports that involve **no foreign exchange transaction at all** need a **waiver from RBI**.

items.title: Export finance in two stages: before and after the ship sails
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before shipment: pre-shipment finance**
- Also called **packing credit** (PCL or EPC).
- A **working capital advance** to **buy, process or make** the goods and to pay **packing, local transport and labour**.
- The borrower normally needs a **firm export order or an export letter of credit**, and the loan is **repaid from the export proceeds**.
- Types: **export packing credit**, and **advances against government receivables** such as **duty drawback**.

**After shipment: post-shipment finance**
- Finance against the **export bills**.
- Types: bills **purchased, discounted or negotiated**; bills **sent on collection**; advances against **consignment** exports; against **undrawn balances**; against **duty drawback**.

Purpose of both: credit at **internationally comparable interest rates**, so exporters can compete.

items.core_explanation_md:
Older books say a packing credit should not exceed **180 days** and may stretch to **360**. RBI's consolidated directions (Chapter XV, from November 2025) say it differently.

- **Period**: the **bank decides** it, case by case, based on the time to procure, make and ship.
- **The hard stop**: if the advance is not **adjusted by export documents within 360 days** of the advance, it **stops qualifying as export credit, from the start (ab initio)**.
- **If no export happens at all**: the bank charges the **domestic lending rate plus any penal charges** under a Board-approved policy.
- **Separate account** for each packing credit, to watch period and end-use.
- **Rate**: banks follow RBI's interest-rate directions, not the old **MCLR** rule of April 2016 in the courseware.

items.title: Paying off packing credit: bills first, flexibility for the trusted
items.core_explanation_md:
**The normal route**: the packing credit is **liquidated from the proceeds of the export bills** on purchase or discount. This **converts pre-shipment credit into post-shipment credit**.

**Other sources, by agreement**: balances in the **EEFC account**, and the exporter's **rupee resources** to the extent exports have actually taken place.

**Relaxations for good track records**
- **Substitution of contract**: liquidate from documents of **another order or commodity**, where it is **commercially necessary and unavoidable**.
- **Mark off** packing credit with proceeds of documents on which **no packing credit** was drawn, after checking **no other bank** gave packing credit for them.

**Never** for **sister, associate or group concerns**.

items.title: The running account: packing credit before the order arrives
items.core_explanation_md:
Normally a bank lends against a **firm order or letter of credit**. Where raw materials are **seasonal**, or manufacture takes longer than the delivery schedule, it may extend a **running account** and lend **before the order is in hand**.

**Who**: exporters with a **good track record**, and **EOUs and units in free trade zones, export processing zones and SEZs**. **Not sub-suppliers**.

**Conditions**
- The **order or LC must be produced within a reasonable time**.
- Export bills are marked off against the **earliest outstanding advance, first in first out**, within the **sanctioned period or 360 days**, whichever is earlier.
- **Misuse** means the facility is withdrawn at once; non-compliance means the advance is **not export credit ab initio**.
