items.title: After shipment: how long, and what about the undrawn balance?
items.core_explanation_md:
**Demand bills**: credit runs for the **Normal Transit Period (NTP)**, a period fixed by **FEDAI**.

**Usance bills**: credit for **at most 365 days from the shipment date**, **including** the NTP and any grace period. The bank must **monitor the need** for the full period and **press exporters to realise early**.

**Overdue bills**: an exporter may clear overdue post-shipment credit from **rupee resources** to cut the interest cost, but the **EDF stays outstanding** and the bill is **still followed up** and reported in **EDPMS**.

**Undrawn balance**: in some trades the bill is drawn for only **90 to 98%** of FOB, the rest paid after the buyer checks quality or quantity. That balance is **contingent**, so the bank may lend against it on **commercial judgement** and the **buyer's record**.

items.title: Export credit in foreign currency: PCFC and EBR
items.core_explanation_md:
**PCFC (pre-shipment credit in foreign currency)**
- For **domestic and imported inputs**, at a rate the bank sets using a widely accepted **Alternative Reference Rate (ARR)** (LIBOR has gone).
- **Cash exports only**; any **convertible currency**, even one different from the invoice (the **cross-currency risk is the exporter's**); **ACU** exports included.
- Funded from **EEFC, RFC(D), FCNR(B)** balances, escrow accounts, overseas lines of credit, or **swaps**.
- If the exporter has **supplier's credit** for imported inputs, PCFC covers **domestic inputs only**.
- **Maximum 360 days**.

**EBR (export bills rediscounted)**
- Post-shipment credit in foreign currency, normally for **usance bills up to 180 days** from shipment, inclusive of transit and grace; longer if the borrower may draw longer usance.
- Bills rediscounted abroad **with recourse** count for export credit performance; **without recourse** do not.

items.title: The Gold Card: fewer hurdles for exporters with a good record
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who gets one**: creditworthy exporters with a **good track record**, MSMEs included, on **criteria each bank sets**. **Not** exporters on ECGC's **Specific Approval List**, or with **overdue bills above 10% of the previous year's turnover**.

**What holders get**
- **Better terms**, with interest **not above the bank's general export credit rate**.
- **Simpler, faster processing**: fresh applications in **25 days**, renewals in **15 days**, ad hoc limits in **7 days**.
- **In-principle limits for three years**, with automatic renewal.
- A **stand-by limit of at least 20% of the assessed limit** for sudden orders.
- **Relaxed inventory norms** for unanticipated orders.
- **Preference in PCFC**, lower fees, and possible **waiver of collateral** and ECGC ECIB cover.

items.title: EDPMS: one screen for every export bill
items.core_explanation_md:
The **Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS)** has run since **1 March 2014**. It gives authorised dealer banks **one platform** to report and monitor exports.

It **brings together** what used to be separate returns on:
- shipping bills of **caution-listed** exporters;
- **delayed use** of advances received for exports;
- exports **outstanding beyond the stipulated period**.

Banks record in it: **advance remittances** for exports, **extensions of time** for realisation, and **write-offs**. They no longer send a separate return for bills outstanding too long: the data is visible in EDPMS.

Banks also keep an **Export Bills Register**, in line with EDPMS, **numbering bills April to March**.

items.title: Chasing overdue export bills, and the caution list
items.core_explanation_md:
**The bank's duty**: watch every bill. If it is **overdue**, take it up with the exporter. If the exporter does not **deliver the proceeds or ask for an extension** in time, **report to the Reserve Bank's Regional Office**, with the reason if known.

**Documents**: the **duplicate EDF or SOFTEX** stays with the bank until **full realisation** (except for undrawn balances).

**Consequence of laxity**: seen **seriously** by RBI; **FEMA penal provisions** may be invoked.

**Caution list**: the RBI lists an exporter **on the bank's recommendation** where the exporter has come to the adverse notice of the **ED, CBI, DRI** or another agency, is **not traceable**, or is **not making sincere efforts** to realise proceeds. The bank also recommends **de-listing**. A caution-listed exporter is told of the listing and the outstanding shipping bills, and bills are accepted only on conditions.

items.title: Factoring: a service that buys the invoices and runs the ledger
items.core_explanation_md:
**What**: an ongoing arrangement where a **factor buys an exporter's book debts** from **open account** sales, **with or without recourse**, and manages credit control and the **sales ledger**.

**Three services**
1. **Debt administration**: keeps the ledger, chases payment.
2. **Credit protection**: assesses buyers' credit.
3. **Factor financing**: advances **75% to 80%** of the outstanding invoices.

**International chain**: exporter → **export factor** (finances) → **import factor** in the buyer's country (collects on the due date and remits). If the debtor does **not pay**, the import factor **steps into the export factor's shoes** to recover.

**Systems**: **single factor**; **two factor**; **direct export** factoring; **direct import** factoring.

**Why exporters use it**: immediate finance, **no letter of credit**, credit checks, ledger work done, credit protection and advice on new markets.

items.title: Forfaiting: selling a medium-term receivable for cash, with no come-back
items.core_explanation_md:
**What**: the financier **discounts** medium-term export receivables **without recourse** to the exporter, at a **fixed rate**, for the **full value**.

**Not insurance**: it is **finance**. The forfaiter judges the **importer's standing**, the **country risk**, and often relies on the **guarantee of the importer's bank**.

**The paper**: a **bill of exchange or promissory note** accepted by the importer and **guaranteed (avalised) by its bank**.

**What it costs**
- **Commitment fee**: usually **0.50% to 1.50% a year** on the unutilised part, **non-refundable**.
- **Discount charge**: a **market-related** rate for the period **plus a margin** for risk.
- **Documentation fees**.

**Benefits to the exporter**: **political and commercial risk** removed, **100% finance**, **no recourse**, no collection work, no credit insurance cost, **fixed rate**.

items.title: Paying for imports on time: the six-month rule and interest
items.core_explanation_md:
**Standard rule**: the importer should **complete remittance within six months of the date of shipment**, unless money is **withheld as a performance guarantee**.

**When payment is late**: the bank may permit settlement of dues **delayed by disputes or financial difficulties**. **Interest** on delayed payments or usance bills may be paid only for **less than three years from the shipment date**, at the **rate prescribed for trade credit**.

**Prepaying a usance bill**: the remittance is made **after deducting the interest for the unexpired part** of the usance.

items.title: Extending the time to pay an import bill: the import version of the rule
items.core_explanation_md:
An importer who cannot pay on time may ask the bank for an **extension**. The bank can grant **up to six months at a time**, to a **maximum of three years**, whatever the invoice value, if the delay is due to **disputes** about quantity or quality, **financial difficulty**, or a **suit** against the seller.

**Checks**: the invoices are **not under investigation** by the Enforcement Directorate, CBI or others; and, for an extension **beyond one year from remittance**, the importer's **total outstanding** must not exceed **USD 1 million or 10% of average import remittances over the previous two financial years, whichever is lower**.

Compare with exporters: the export test is **whichever is higher** (USD 1 million or 10% of three years' realisations). The import test is **whichever is lower**, over **two** years. **Beyond the limits**: the bank refers to the **RBI Regional Office**. Every extension is **reported in IDPMS**.

items.title: Paying a supplier in advance: when a guarantee is needed
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank may allow an **advance remittance for imports without any overall ceiling**, on these conditions:

- **Up to USD 2,00,000**: no guarantee.
- **Above USD 2,00,000**: an **unconditional, irrevocable standby letter of credit** or a **guarantee** from an international bank of repute (or from an Indian bank issued against that bank's counter-guarantee).
- **Exception for private importers**: if the importer **cannot** get the guarantee and the bank is satisfied about its **track record and bona fides**, the guarantee **need not be insisted on up to USD 5 million**, under a **Board-approved policy**.
- **Public sector and government bodies**: a **specific waiver from the Ministry of Finance** is needed before remitting **more than USD 1,00,000** without a guarantee.

The bank creates an **ORM** in IDPMS for **every** such remittance.

items.title: When a CEO's certificate can replace the bill of entry
items.core_explanation_md:
Normally the importer shows the **exchange control copy of the bill of entry**. In place of it a bank may accept a **certificate from the CEO or auditor** that the goods have really been imported, **if both** hold:

- **less than USD 10,00,000** (one million) was remitted; and
- the importer is a **listed company with net worth of at least ₹100 crore** at its last audited balance sheet, **or** a **public sector company** or government undertaking.

The facility can also be extended to **autonomous bodies audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General**, such as scientific bodies and academic institutions. At **EDI ports** the bank downloads the bill of entry from the **BoE Master in IDPMS** and creates an **ORM**.

items.title: Financing imports, and the system that tracks them
items.core_explanation_md:
**Import letter of credit (usance)**: the importer gets **credit from the supplier** on the strength of the **bank's credibility**.

**Import loan**: a loan against **imported raw material or goods for trading**, secured by **pledge or hypothecation**; importers use them even at higher rates, waiting for prices to rise or the rupee to fall.

**Supplier's credit** vs **buyer's credit**
- **Supplier's credit**: **the overseas supplier** lends directly to the importer.
- **Buyer's credit**: the **importer arranges** a loan from a **bank or institution abroad** to pay the supplier **on immediate terms**.

**IDPMS (Import Data Processing and Monitoring System)**, in use from **10 October 2016**: customs, RBI and banks share one platform. **Customs data from the bill of entry** flows to the system and on to the bank **by its AD code**. The bank records **each step** (document submission, remittance data) **in real time**. **No separate Bill of Entry statement** is filed.

items.title: Trade credit: how long it may last
items.core_explanation_md:
Any **deferred payment arrangement** for imports, including **supplier's and buyer's credit**, is a **trade credit** if it runs for:

- up to **three years** for **capital goods**; or
- up to **one year or the operating cycle, whichever is shorter**, for **non-capital goods**.

Trade credits follow the **Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations**, not the ordinary import payment rules.

(How much a bank may approve per import, and what the **all-in cost** may be, are set in that Master Direction. Those figures have moved with the LIBOR transition and are not tested here.)
